stages.content:
# Kali Linux Setup & Basics

## Why this lesson exists

Kali is a **security workstation**, not permission. Installing tools does not authorize you to touch systems. The first professional skill is setting up a repeatable lab, naming the authorized target, and recording what each tool run is meant to prove.

In this lesson you will create a lab note that names workspace, authorized target, purpose, and cleanup before any scan or exploit language enters the conversation.

This card is a focused **20–25 hour** introduction to Kali lab hygiene. A longer zero-to-job-ready path exists outside this course; do not treat this card as that full path.

## Where this course sits

This course teaches **lab workstation and tool craft** inside a controlled Kali environment: setup, safe workflows, evidence handling, and documentation under scope. It complements — it does not replace — **Ethical Hacking & Penetration Testing**, which covers full assessment methodology end-to-end. Pick Kali when you need to operate tools carefully; pair with Ethical Hacking for the engagement process from scope through reporting and defender handoff. Practice only against **authorized local lab** targets you name in writing. Kali is a workstation, not permission.

## Reminder: where you work

Create a course notes folder on your machine (or inside your Kali / lab VM):

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-01
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-01
```

Windows (PowerShell on the host, or WSL if that is your lab shell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-01"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-01"
```

You will write `lab_note.txt` (or a short shell script that prints the same fields) in that folder. Prefer a **dedicated lab VM** with snapshots so mistakes stay contained.

## Start here: scope before shell

Do not open tools and hunt for interesting output. Write the operating boundary first:

1. Where do notes and temporary files live?
2. What authorized target label may be touched?
3. Why would a future tool run be useful?
4. How will temporary lab files be cleaned up?

You are not proving exploitation yet. You are making Kali work **reviewable** so an instructor, teammate, or future you can tell what was allowed, what was touched, and why.

## Workstation boundary

| Item | Purpose | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace | Keeps notes and evidence together | A folder is not a target |
| Authorized target | Names the lab system that can be touched | Visibility ≠ permission |
| Tool purpose | Explains why a command would be run | Purpose is not a finding |
| Cleanup note | Prevents stale files from becoming confusing evidence | Cleanup must be real, not aspirational |

First say the boundary in one sentence: *this workstation may only create a lab note for the named target, with a stated purpose and cleanup rule.*

## Lab setup habits that matter early

| Habit | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Snapshot or backup before practice | You can recover when a package or config break happens |
| Separate notes / evidence / scratch | Scratch files do not look like proof later |
| Label targets as lab hosts | Reduces accidental public-system contact |
| Record tool purpose before output | Stops “interesting output” from rewriting the plan |
| Prefer host-only or isolated lab networks | Limits blast radius |

If you run Kali in a VM, treat the guest as the workstation and the host notes folder (or a synced lab folder) as the evidence shelf. Do not practice against production, neighbors’ Wi‑Fi, or random internet hosts.

## Scope sentence patterns

Use plain language. Examples for authorized practice only:

```text
Authorized: lab.local (Metasploitable / DVWA / custom lab VM on host-only network)
Purpose: document discovery workflow for that labeled target
Out of scope: any host not named in this note
Cleanup: delete /tmp lab scratch files after notes are saved
```

Bad scope: “whatever shows up in nmap.” Good scope: one named lab label plus an explicit out-of-scope line.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Opening tools before naming the authorized target
- Treating a public hostname as “practice” because it is interesting
- Saving evidence only in `/tmp` with no durable note
- Skipping cleanup so the next session inherits junk as “evidence”
- Confusing Kali installation success with authorization
- Expecting an automatic grading inside the lesson instead of writing a local lab note

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Confirm lab context

Write three lines in a scratch file:

```text
workstation=kali-lab-vm (or your authorized lab host)
network=host-only / isolated lab (name yours)
authorized_target=lab.local
```

If you cannot name those honestly, stop and fix the lab setup before any tool practice.

### Step 2 — Write the lab note

Create `lab_note.txt`:

```text
workspace=/home/kali/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-01
authorized_target=lab.local
tool_purpose=document safe discovery workflow for an authorized lab target
cleanup_note=remove temporary lab notes from /tmp after practice; keep this lab_note.txt
out_of_scope=any host not labeled lab.local
```

Optional: print the same fields from a shell script in your lab folder:

```bash
workspace="$HOME/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-01"
authorized_target="lab.local"
tool_purpose="document safe discovery workflow for an authorized lab target"
cleanup_note="remove temporary lab notes from /tmp after practice; keep lab_note.txt"
out_of_scope="any host not labeled lab.local"

mkdir -p "$workspace"
printf '%s\n' \
  "workspace=$workspace" \
  "target=$authorized_target" \
  "purpose=$tool_purpose" \
  "cleanup=$cleanup_note" \
  "out_of_scope=$out_of_scope"
```

### Step 3 — Self-review

Read the note as if you are the next reviewer. Ask:

- Can I see what is allowed without guessing?
- Is the target a lab label, not a random public system?
- Would cleanup leave durable notes and remove scratch?

### Step 4 — One change you can explain

Change **one** field (purpose or cleanup) and say out loud why the new wording makes the next session safer or clearer.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Workstation | Where you run tools (often a Kali VM) |
| Authorized target | The only system you may actively test |
| Scope | Written boundary of what is in / out |
| Lab note | Pre-run record of workspace, target, purpose, cleanup |
| Evidence | Saved output tied to a stated purpose |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] Course notes folder exists for stage-01
- [ ] `lab_note.txt` lists workspace, authorized target, purpose, cleanup, out of scope
- [ ] Target is a lab label, not a random public host
- [ ] You can explain the note in under one minute
- [ ] You know practice is local / authorized lab only (no automatic grading inside the lesson)

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Use only systems you own, systems in your isolated lab, or systems you are explicitly authorized to test. Do not scan, probe, or collect from real third-party systems without written permission.

When those items are true, continue to **Information Gathering Tools**.

stages.title: Information Gathering Tools

quiz.question: What separates passive reconnaissance from active reconnaissance?
options: Whether the target system is contacted
Whether the notes are short
Whether Kali is installed
Whether the result looks interesting
quiz.explanation: Active reconnaissance sends traffic or queries to a target, so it must stay inside scope.

quiz.question: A useful recon clue automatically means you may scan any related host. True or false?
options: True — discovery equals permission
False — the next action must stay on the authorized target
True — if confidence is high
False — unless the tool name is famous
quiz.explanation: Evidence supports a hypothesis; authorization and written scope decide contact.

quiz.question: Why record confidence in a recon log?
options: To make the log longer for grading
To justify scanning out-of-scope networks
To keep weak clues from becoming overstated claims
To replace the evidence note
quiz.explanation: Honest confidence prevents turning thin sources into certainty.

stages.content:
# Information Gathering Tools

## Why this lesson exists

Information gathering is not a tool list. It is a plan for collecting evidence while separating **passive observation** from **active target contact**.

In this lesson you will write a recon log entry that names source, authorized target, evidence, confidence, and the next action that stays inside scope.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-02
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-02
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-02"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-02"
```

You will write `recon_log.txt` in that folder. Keep any active checks limited to the authorized lab target named in Stage 01.

## Start here: evidence before contact

Do not treat a discovered clue as permission to touch a system. First answer:

1. Where did the clue come from (passive source)?
2. What authorized target may be checked actively?
3. What does the evidence actually prove?
4. How confident should you be?
5. What next action stays inside scope?

Good reconnaissance keeps the line visible between what was observed and what may be contacted.

## Passive versus active

| Mode | What it means | Example (lab only) | Scope note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Passive | No direct contact with the target | Reading public docs you already control, lab DNS notes, prior engagement records | Still respect privacy and legality |
| Active | Sends traffic or queries to the target | Authorized `nmap` against `lab.local` | Requires explicit authorization |

A useful clue is not automatically permission to scan, browse, or test. The next action must be tied to the approved lab target and the evidence already collected.

## Recon evidence model

| Field | Why it matters | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Passive source | Shows where the clue came from | Source quality varies |
| Active target | Keeps follow-up inside authorization | Must match the written scope |
| Evidence note | Records what the source actually proves | Do not exaggerate |
| Confidence | Prevents weak clues from becoming claims | Medium is often honest |
| Next action | Connects evidence to an allowed step | Action must stay in scope |

First say the recon boundary in one sentence: *this clue came from a named source, applies to a named authorized target, and only supports the next scoped action.*

## Tool mindset (not a shopping list)

Common Kali recon families include DNS helpers, web discovery utilities, and OSINT-style collectors. Names change; the professional habit does not:

1. Name the question before the tool.
2. Prefer passive notes when they answer the question.
3. Escalate to active checks only against the authorized target.
4. Log confidence and next action before chasing more noise.

If a tool returns dozens of hostnames, your job is not to chase all of them. Your job is to keep the log tied to `lab.local` (or your written label) and discard out-of-scope noise.

## Confidence language

| Level | When to use it | What to avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low | Single weak clue, unverified | “Confirmed host” |
| Medium | Two consistent clues, still unverified | Claiming vulnerability |
| High | Verified against the authorized target with repeatable evidence | Skipping the verification step |

## Common beginner mistakes

- Treating discovery as permission
- Running active checks against anything “interesting”
- Logging tool names instead of what was proven
- Setting confidence to high because the output looked cool
- Skipping the next-action field so the log becomes a dead pile of text
- Assuming ASV Learn will auto-grade your recon log

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Capture a sample clue

Use this authorized practice scenario (synthetic lab data):

```text
Passive source: lab DNS notes and internal engagement brief
Clue: lab.local is the approved training target for web service discovery
Active target allowed: lab.local only
Not allowed: neighbor hosts, public internet targets, unrelated SSIDs
```

### Step 2 — Write the recon log

Create `recon_log.txt`:

```text
passive_source=lab DNS notes and engagement brief
active_target=lab.local
evidence_note=records name lab.local as the approved training target for discovery
confidence=medium
next_authorized_action=run active checks only against lab.local on the isolated lab network
out_of_scope=any host not labeled lab.local
```

Optional shell print:

```bash
passive_source="lab DNS notes and engagement brief"
active_target="lab.local"
evidence_note="records name lab.local as the approved training target for discovery"
confidence="medium"
next_authorized_action="run active checks only against lab.local on the isolated lab network"

printf '%s\n' \
  "passive_source=$passive_source" \
  "active_target=$active_target" \
  "evidence=$evidence_note" \
  "confidence=$confidence" \
  "next_action=$next_authorized_action"
```

### Step 3 — Self-review

- Does the next action contact only the authorized target?
- Is confidence honest about what the source proves?
- Would a second person know what is out of scope?

### Step 4 — One change you can explain

Lower or raise confidence by one step and rewrite one sentence so the next action still matches the evidence.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Passive recon | Observation without contacting the target |
| Active recon | Checks that contact the target |
| Evidence note | What the source actually shows |
| Confidence | How strongly you trust the clue |
| Next action | The allowed follow-up inside scope |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `recon_log.txt` lists source, target, evidence, confidence, next action, out of scope
- [ ] Passive and active are separated in your wording
- [ ] Next action stays on the authorized lab target
- [ ] Confidence is not inflated
- [ ] Practice stays on local / authorized lab only

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Do not gather information against real organizations, people, or networks without written authorization. Lab practice uses synthetic data and systems you control or are approved to test.

When those items are true, continue to **Scanning & Enumeration Tools**.

stages.title: Scanning & Enumeration Tools

quiz.question: What does an open port prove by itself?
options: The host is compromised
A reachable service may exist
A critical vulnerability exists
The report is complete
quiz.explanation: Open ports are inventory clues. Vulnerability claims require more evidence.

quiz.question: What belongs in a professional service inventory row?
options: Host, port, likely service, confidence, and a safe verification step
Only the tool command that produced the loudest output
A list of every host on the local broadcast domain
An exploit name before verification
quiz.explanation: Inventory rows preserve what was observed and what still needs verification.

quiz.question: Where may you run active scanners for this course?
options: Against any host that answers ping
Against public websites that load slowly
Only against authorized lab hosts you control or have written permission to test
Against any host that answers on your local Wi‑Fi
quiz.explanation: Unauthorized scanning can be illegal and harmful; practice stays in authorized labs.

quiz.question: Why prefer a focused port list on one labeled lab host while learning?
options: Wide subnet sweeps always produce better findings
Focused scans create clearer inventory and less accidental out-of-scope contact
Focused scans remove the need for notes
Tool defaults already guarantee authorization
quiz.explanation: Beginners learn faster and safer by mapping one authorized host carefully.

stages.content:
# Scanning & Enumeration Tools

## Why this lesson exists

Scanning produces **inventory evidence**. It does not automatically prove a vulnerability. A professional service note separates host, port, likely service, confidence, and the next safe verification step.

In this lesson you will build a small **service inventory** for an authorized lab host: at least two rows that treat scan output as a map, not a verdict.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-03
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-03
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-03"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-03"
```

You will write `service_inventory.txt`. Any real scanner practice must stay on `lab.local` (or your written authorized label) on an isolated lab network. Keep Stage 01’s lab note nearby.

## Start here: inventory before conclusions

Do not turn scan output into a finding. First name:

1. Authorized host
2. Port
3. Likely service
4. Confidence
5. One safe verification step

A port, banner, or service guess is inventory. It becomes useful when you can explain what it proves, what it does not prove, and what still needs verification.

## Networking facts that keep scans honest

You do not need a full networking textbook for this stage, but you do need these distinctions when reading Kali scan tools:

| Idea | Why it matters in the lab |
| --- | --- |
| Host discovery | “Is this address worth scanning?” is different from “what ports are open?” |
| TCP vs UDP | Open UDP is harder to interpret; silence is not always “closed” |
| Port states | Open, closed, filtered, and unknown are different evidence qualities |
| Banner / version clues | Helpful hypotheses; often wrong, incomplete, or intentionally misleading |
| Timing and noise | Faster scans are louder; lab timing still belongs in your notes |

If your lab uses host-only networking, write that down. Bridged adapters make accidental contact with non-lab hosts much easier.

## Inventory row model

| Field | Example | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Host | lab.local | Must be in scope |
| Port | 443 | Open ≠ vulnerable |
| Likely service | https | Banner can lie or be incomplete |
| Confidence | medium | Guessed services stay medium/low |
| Next safe check | verify TLS cert / banner on authorized host | Check must stay scoped |

One sentence check: *host, port, likely service, confidence, and one safe verification step.*

## Reading scan output professionally

Typical Kali scanning tools (Nmap-family workflows and similar) can show ports, states, and guessed services. Treat the columns like this:

| Output piece | What it is | What it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open port | Reachability clue | Proof of exploitability |
| Service guess | Hypothesis | Confirmed software + version |
| Banner | Hint | Guaranteed truth |
| Many open ports | Wider inventory | Automatic critical finding |
| Script title mentioning a CVE | A clue to review later | A confirmed finding for Stage 04 |

Prefer a small, explained inventory over a huge dump nobody will reread. Save raw tool output under an `evidence/` folder if you keep it, and keep the human rows in `service_inventory.txt`.

## Scan choices that stay reviewable

| Approach | Typical lab use | What it proves | What it does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Host discovery | Confirm `lab.local` is up | Reachability clue | Softness of the host |
| Focused TCP ports | Map likely service entry points | Possible listeners | Exploitability |
| Version detection | Guess product/version | Stronger service hypothesis | Confirmed CVE |
| Manual banner grab | Read one service carefully | Exact observed text | That the text is trustworthy |

Prefer a narrow authorized scan over a wide “everything” run while you are still learning the inventory habit.

## Safe verification steps

Good next checks stay narrow and authorized:

- Confirm the service banner on the same authorized host
- Note whether the service matches the engagement purpose
- Record version only when the tool actually returns it
- Avoid exploitation language in this stage

Bad next checks:

- “Try exploits”
- “Scan the whole subnet I can see”
- “Test the neighbor’s printer”

## Common beginner mistakes

- Calling an open port a vulnerability
- Trusting version-detection guesses as facts
- Expanding scope because more hosts answered
- Pasting raw scanner walls into a report without a human row
- Skipping confidence so every line looks equally certain
- Expecting ASV Learn to run Nmap inside the lesson page

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Name the authorized scan target

Write the top of `service_inventory.txt`:

```text
authorized_target=lab.local
scan_purpose=build service inventory for authorized lab host
out_of_scope=any host not labeled lab.local
network=host-only / isolated lab
```

### Step 2 — Run one scoped inventory action

If nmap is available in your Kali/lab VM and scope allows it, prefer a focused command against the labeled host:

```bash
mkdir -p evidence
nmap -sV -p 22,80,443 lab.local -oN evidence/nmap-lab-local.txt
```

If nmap is not available, use an authorized manual check you can explain:

```bash
nc -vz lab.local 80
```

Replace host and ports with your labeled lab values. Do not invent a public target.

### Step 3 — Write at least two inventory rows

Append durable rows to `service_inventory.txt` (edit for your real output):

```text
host=lab.local
port=22
likely_service=ssh
confidence=medium
evidence=port open; SSH-style banner observed; version not confirmed
next_safe_check=record banner text; do not attempt credential guessing yet

host=lab.local
port=443
likely_service=https
confidence=medium
evidence=port open; service guess https; version not confirmed
next_safe_check=verify the service banner and certificate subject on lab.local only
```

Optional shell print for one row:

```bash
host="lab.local"
port="443"
likely_service="https"
confidence="medium"
next_safe_check="verify the service banner against the authorized lab host"

printf '%s\n' \
  "host=$host" \
  "port=$port" \
  "service=$likely_service" \
  "confidence=$confidence" \
  "next_check=$next_safe_check"
```

### Step 4 — Self-review

- Did you avoid calling either row a vulnerability?
- Is each next check safe and in scope?
- Could a defender use these rows as a starting inventory?

### Step 5 — One change you can explain

Change confidence or `next_safe_check` on one row and say why the new wording better matches the evidence.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Scan | Active check that maps reachable services |
| Enumeration | Gathering more detail about a service |
| Inventory | Structured list of observed services |
| Banner | Text a service returns that may hint identity |
| Verification | Narrow follow-up that confirms or weakens a guess |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `service_inventory.txt` names authorized target and out-of-scope line
- [ ] At least two ports/services are recorded with evidence
- [ ] Each row has confidence and a safe next step
- [ ] Open ports are treated as inventory, not compromise
- [ ] Scan commands stayed on the labeled lab host
- [ ] Practice is local / authorized lab only

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Do not scan networks or hosts you do not own or have written permission to test. Unauthorized scanning can be illegal and harmful.

When those items are true, continue to **Vulnerability Assessment**.

stages.title: Vulnerability Assessment

quiz.question: What makes a vulnerability finding useful?
options: Evidence, impact, and remediation
Only the scanner title
A dramatic label
A list of unrelated tools
quiz.explanation: Defenders need proof, impact, and a practical remediation path.

quiz.question: Why is pasting scanner language into a report a beginner mistake?
options: Scanners are never useful
Reports should never mention versions
Scanner titles still need human review against a specific asset and evidence
Remediation should be hidden from defenders
quiz.explanation: Assessment turns signals into defender-facing findings with asset, evidence, and fix path.

quiz.question: When evidence only shows an old banner without package confirmation, what confidence fits best?
options: Critical certainty
Medium or low until version is verified
No confidence field is needed
High, because banners never lie
quiz.explanation: Unverified version matches stay medium/low so impact is not overstated.

stages.content:
# Vulnerability Assessment

## Why this lesson exists

Vulnerability assessment turns signals into actionable findings. A useful finding connects **asset**, **evidence**, **impact**, **confidence**, and **remediation** — not scanner marketing language.

In this lesson you will write one vulnerability triage row a defender could verify and fix.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-04
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-04
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-04"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-04"
```

You will write `vuln_triage.txt`. Keep any scanner practice on the authorized lab asset only.

## Start here: review before finding

Do not paste scanner language into a report. First name:

1. Affected asset
2. Signal
3. Supporting evidence
4. Impact (honest)
5. Remediation or verification path
6. Confidence

The useful skill is turning a signal into something a defender can check and fix. Specific enough to act on; careful enough not to overstate.

## From signal to finding

| Field | Reviewer question | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asset | What system or service is affected? | Must be in scope |
| Signal | What suggested the issue? | Signal ≠ confirmed flaw |
| Evidence | What supports the finding? | Need more than a title |
| Impact | Why should a defender care? | Avoid drama |
| Remediation | What practical fix or verify step exists? | Must be actionable |
| Confidence | How sure are you? | Unverified stays medium/low |

First say the triage row in one sentence: *asset, signal, evidence, impact, and remediation or verification path.*

## Scanner output needs a human

Tools such as OpenVAS, Nessus-style reports, or Nikto-class web scanners can produce long result lists. Your job in this card:

1. Pick **one** signal worth review.
2. Tie it to one asset in the authorized lab.
3. Write evidence in defender language.
4. Offer a fix or verify step.
5. Leave unrelated noise out of the triage row.

| Trap | Better move |
| --- | --- |
| “Critical” because the scanner said so | Re-check evidence and version match |
| Copying CVE titles with no asset | Name host/service first |
| Impact as “total compromise” for every item | Match impact to what evidence supports |
| No remediation | Give update, config, or verify steps |

## Impact without exaggeration

| Evidence quality | Impact wording style |
| --- | --- |
| Banner suggests old version, CVE not confirmed | “Possible exposure if version matches a known weakness — verify package version” |
| Confirmed outdated package with known issue in lab | “Lab service runs version X associated with issue Y — patch and retest” |
| Theoretical only | Keep in review; do not promote to confirmed finding |

## Common beginner mistakes

- Pasting scanner titles as findings
- Skipping asset identity
- Inflating impact for attention
- Offering no remediation path
- Mixing many unrelated signals into one row
- Treating this lesson as an auto-graded exploit exercise instead of writing a triage row

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Sample signal

Authorized synthetic sample:

```text
Asset: lab-web on lab.local
Signal: outdated server banner
Evidence: scanner result and service banner both point to an old version string
Missing: package inventory confirmation on the host
```

### Step 2 — Gather one verification clue (authorized lab only)

If your Stage 03 inventory already has a version or banner for `lab.local`, copy that evidence into this stage. Optional focused check:

```bash
mkdir -p evidence
# Example only — replace with your labeled service/port
curl -sI https://lab.local/ | tee evidence/lab-local-headers.txt
```

If the lab app is HTTP-only, use `http://lab.local/` instead. Do not point this at a public third-party host.

### Step 3 — Write the triage row

Create `vuln_triage.txt`:

```text
asset=lab-web on lab.local
vulnerability_signal=outdated server banner
evidence=scanner result and service banner both point to an old version string
impact=possible exposure if the version matches a confirmed weakness
confidence=medium
remediation=confirm package version on the lab host; update the package; re-check the banner after patching
verification=defender can compare pre/post banner and package version
```

Optional shell print:

```bash
asset="lab-web"
vulnerability_signal="outdated server banner"
evidence="scanner result and service banner both point to an old version"
impact="possible exposure if the version has a matching confirmed weakness"
remediation="update the package and verify the service after patching"

printf '%s\n' \
  "asset=$asset" \
  "signal=$vulnerability_signal" \
  "evidence=$evidence" \
  "impact=$impact" \
  "remediation=$remediation"
```

### Step 4 — Self-review

- Could a defender verify this without guessing which host you meant?
- Is impact matched to evidence?
- Is remediation practical in a lab?

### Step 5 — One change you can explain

Adjust confidence or impact wording so it better matches what is actually proven.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Signal | Something that suggests a possible issue |
| Finding | Reviewed claim with evidence and impact |
| Triage | Choosing what matters and what stays in review |
| Remediation | Fix or verify path a defender can take |
| False positive | Signal that does not hold after review |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `vuln_triage.txt` includes asset, signal, evidence, impact, remediation, confidence
- [ ] Wording is defender-facing, not scanner marketing
- [ ] Impact is not exaggerated past the evidence
- [ ] One signal per row
- [ ] Practice stays on authorized lab assets only

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Run vulnerability scanners only against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to assess. Unauthorized scanning can disrupt services and violate law or policy.

When those items are true, continue to **Web Application Testing**.

# Web Application Testing

## Why this lesson exists

Web testing starts by understanding how the application communicates. The request **method**, **path**, **parameter**, **expected response**, and **observed response** become the basis for safe test cases.

In this lesson you will write a web test note that records normal behavior before proposing a scoped follow-up test.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-05
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-05
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-05"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-05"
```

You will write `web_test_note.txt`. Point any proxy or browser tools only at your authorized lab application URL.

## Start here: baseline before tests

Do not change input until normal behavior is clear. First name:

1. HTTP method
2. Request path
3. User-controlled parameter
4. Expected response
5. Observed response
6. Next safe test

When you know what normal looks like, unusual behavior can be compared without drifting outside the lab application.

## Request shape

| Field | Purpose | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP method | Shows the request action | Method alone is not a bug |
| Request path | Names the endpoint | Path must be in-scope lab app |
| User parameter | Identifies controllable input | Not every parameter is sensitive |
| Expected response | Defines normal behavior | Expectation must be written first |
| Observed response | Captures what happened | Observation ≠ exploit proof |
| Next safe test | Keeps follow-up tied to evidence | Must stay inside the lab app |

First say the baseline in one sentence: *method, path, parameter, expected response, observed response, and next safe test.*

## Baseline workflow

1. Load the lab page with a normal request.
2. Note status code, redirect target, or page purpose.
3. Identify one parameter you control (query, form, header if in scope).
4. Write expected vs observed before any payload thinking.
5. Propose one safe follow-up that answers a single question.

| Safe follow-up examples | Unsafe drift |
| --- | --- |
| Confirm redirect stays on lab host | Jump to arbitrary external redirects on live sites |
| Compare response when parameter is empty vs present | Blast large payload lists with no baseline |
| Note whether error messages leak stack traces in lab | Attack third-party production apps |

Tools such as browser DevTools, an intercepting proxy, or curl help you **see** requests. Seeing is not permission to hammer. Keep the note small and reviewable.

## Open redirect style example (lab only)

Synthetic authorized scenario:

```text
Method: GET
Path: /login
Parameter: redirect
Expected: login page or safe local redirect inside the lab app
Observed: 302 to the requested local path
Next safe test: validate the redirect target stays on the lab application host
```

This stage teaches the note, not a full exploit chain. Do not escalate into persistence or data theft narratives here.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Changing inputs before writing expected behavior
- Testing the wrong host because a bookmark pointed elsewhere
- Treating every anomaly as critical
- Skipping the parameter name so nobody can reproduce
- Using public websites as “practice targets”
- Expecting ASV Learn to proxy traffic for you

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Confirm lab app target

Write the authorized URL in a one-line file `target_url.txt`:

```text
https://lab.local/login
```

If that is not a lab you control or are authorized to test, stop.

### Step 2 — Capture a normal baseline request

Against your authorized lab app only, capture one normal response (edit the URL to match `target_url.txt`):

```bash
mkdir -p evidence
curl -sI "https://lab.local/login" | tee evidence/baseline-login-headers.txt
```

Write expected behavior **before** you propose any unusual parameter values.

### Step 3 — Write the web test note

Create `web_test_note.txt`:

```text
http_method=GET
request_path=/login
user_parameter=redirect
expected_response=login page or safe local redirect inside the lab application
observed_response=302 redirect to the requested local path
next_safe_test=validate the redirect stays inside the lab application host
scope=lab.local web app only
```

Optional shell print:

```bash
http_method="GET"
request_path="/login"
user_parameter="redirect"
expected_response="login page or safe local redirect"
observed_response="302 redirect to the requested local path"
next_safe_test="validate the redirect stays inside the lab application"

printf '%s\n' \
  "method=$http_method" \
  "path=$request_path" \
  "parameter=$user_parameter" \
  "expected=$expected_response" \
  "observed=$observed_response" \
  "next_test=$next_safe_test"
```

### Step 4 — Self-review

- Is expected written clearly enough to compare?
- Does the next test stay on the lab app?
- Could another tester reproduce from the note alone?

### Step 5 — One change you can explain

Change one field (parameter or next_safe_test) and explain how the comparison still works.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline | Documented normal behavior |
| Parameter | User-controlled input in the request |
| Observed response | What the server actually returned |
| Safe test | Narrow, authorized follow-up |
| Scope | Lab application boundary |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `target_url.txt` names an authorized lab app
- [ ] `web_test_note.txt` has method, path, parameter, expected, observed, next safe test
- [ ] Expected was written before proposing unusual input
- [ ] Next test stays inside the lab application
- [ ] No public third-party targets were used

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Practice only against intentionally vulnerable lab apps you host (for example DVWA, Juice Shop, or a course lab VM) — never against random public sites.

Web application testing without authorization is illegal. Use intentionally vulnerable labs you host or platforms that explicitly authorize your account for practice.

When those items are true, continue to **Exploitation Techniques**.

stages.content:
# Exploitation Techniques

## Why this lesson exists

In a professional lab, exploitation is **controlled validation** of a confirmed weakness. It is not exploration, persistence, or unnecessary impact.

In this lesson you will write a controlled proof card: finding, precondition, proof goal, impact limit, stop condition, and cleanup.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-06
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-06
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-06"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-06"
```

You will write `controlled_proof_card.txt`. Take a VM snapshot before any validation attempt that might change the lab.

## Start here: proof boundary before validation

Do not treat validation as open-ended exploration. First name:

1. Confirmed finding
2. Precondition (authorization + confirmation)
3. Proof goal (minimum useful evidence)
4. Impact limit (what will not happen)
5. Stop condition
6. Cleanup note

Controlled proof work answers one narrow question and stops. The plan should say what will **not** happen as clearly as what evidence will be captured.

## Controlled proof card

| Field | Boundary | Example wording |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finding | Confirmed issue being validated | “Outdated lab service with verified weak config” |
| Precondition | Authorization and confirmation | “Authorized lab target; signal already triaged” |
| Proof goal | Minimum evidence needed | “Show controlled validation without persistence” |
| Impact limit | What the proof will not do | “No lateral movement, no data theft, no persistence” |
| Stop condition | When activity ends | “Stop after proof output is captured” |
| Cleanup note | Temporary artifacts removed | “Remove proof files; revert snapshot if needed” |

First say the proof boundary in one sentence: *finding, precondition, proof goal, impact limit, stop condition, and cleanup.*

## What “proof” means here

| Acceptable proof goal | Out of bounds for this card |
| --- | --- |
| Demonstrate the weakness exists with minimal impact | Dump databases “for fun” |
| Capture a screenshot or short log proving the issue | Install backdoors |
| Show a safe lab command output tied to the finding | Pivot to other hosts |
| Stop and document | Keep going after the goal is met |

Framework names (Metasploit and similar) are secondary. The professional skill is the boundary card. If you cannot write the card, you are not ready to run a proof.

## Precondition checklist

Before any validation attempt:

- [ ] Written authorization / ownership of the lab target
- [ ] Finding already reviewed (Stage 04 style), not a random guess
- [ ] Snapshot or rollback plan exists
- [ ] Proof goal is one sentence
- [ ] Impact limits are explicit
- [ ] Cleanup owner is you, with a time box

## Common beginner mistakes

- Treating exploitation as exploration
- Continuing after the proof goal is met
- Collecting unnecessary sensitive data in a lab “because you can”
- Skipping cleanup so the next session inherits a dirty lab
- Skipping the precondition of confirmed signal + authorization
- Looking for an in-lesson exploit button that does not exist here

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Name the finding

Use this authorized synthetic scenario (or your real lab finding if already confirmed):

```text
Finding: outdated lab service with weak configuration
Target: lab.local
Authorization: own lab VM / written lab brief
```

### Step 2 — Snapshot gate

Before any validation that might change lab state, write one line you can prove later:

```text
snapshot_taken=yes
snapshot_label=pre-stage-06-proof
rollback_owner=me
```

If you cannot take a snapshot, keep this stage as a **dry-run proof card** and do not run validation commands.

### Step 3 — Write the controlled proof card

Create `controlled_proof_card.txt`:

```text
finding=outdated lab service with weak configuration
precondition=authorized lab target and confirmed vulnerability signal
proof_goal=show controlled validation without persistence or data access
impact_limit=no persistence, no sensitive data access, no lateral movement
stop_condition=stop after proof output is captured
cleanup_note=remove temporary proof files from the lab workspace; restore snapshot if lab state changed
rollback_plan=revert to pre-proof VM snapshot if needed
```

Optional shell print:

```bash
finding="outdated lab service"
precondition="authorized lab target and confirmed vulnerability signal"
proof_goal="show controlled validation without persistence or data access"
impact_limit="no persistence, no sensitive data access, no lateral movement"
stop_condition="stop after proof output is captured"
cleanup_note="remove temporary proof files from the lab workspace"

printf '%s\n' \
  "finding=$finding" \
  "precondition=$precondition" \
  "proof_goal=$proof_goal" \
  "impact_limit=$impact_limit" \
  "stop_condition=$stop_condition" \
  "cleanup=$cleanup_note"
```

### Step 4 — Self-review

- Is the proof goal the smallest useful evidence?
- Are impact limits explicit enough that a teammate could stop you?
- Is cleanup / rollback real?

### Step 5 — One change you can explain

Tighten the proof goal or impact limit by one clause and say why that reduces risk.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Controlled proof | Minimal validation of a confirmed issue |
| Precondition | What must be true before proof work |
| Impact limit | Actions that are forbidden during proof |
| Stop condition | When validation ends |
| Cleanup | Removing temporary artifacts after evidence is saved |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `controlled_proof_card.txt` includes all six core fields plus rollback
- [ ] Proof goal is narrow
- [ ] Impact limits forbid persistence and lateral movement
- [ ] Stop condition is explicit
- [ ] Practice stays on authorized lab targets only

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Keep impact minimal and stop when the proof goal is met. This path does not host exploits.

Exploitation against systems without authorization is illegal. Use only lab systems you own or are explicitly permitted to validate. Prefer snapshots and minimal impact.

When those items are true, continue to **Wireless Testing Tools**.

# Wireless Testing Tools

## Why this lesson exists

Wireless testing uses shared radio space, so scope must be explicit. Nearby networks and unrelated clients are **not** targets just because they appear in tool output.

In this lesson you will write a wireless test card that names authorized SSID, channel, approved hardware, capture purpose, privacy rule, and cleanup.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-07
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-07
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-07"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-07"
```

You will write `wireless_test_card.txt`. If you lack an authorized lab SSID and compatible adapter, complete this stage as a **documentation-only** lab using the sample fields — do not capture neighbor traffic.

## Start here: authorization before wireless capture

Do not treat visible networks as targets. First name:

1. Authorized SSID
2. Channel
3. Approved hardware
4. Capture purpose
5. Privacy rule
6. Cleanup note

Wireless work needs extra care because unrelated people and devices may be nearby. The lab card should make non-lab networks and clients explicitly out of scope.

## Radio scope card

| Field | Reason | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authorized SSID | Names the target network | Visibility ≠ authorization |
| Channel | Limits radio context | Other channels may still show noise |
| Approved hardware | Confirms the lab adapter | Wrong adapter → skip capture |
| Capture purpose | Explains why data is recorded | Purpose must be narrow |
| Privacy rule | Excludes unrelated networks/users | Must be enforced in practice |
| Cleanup note | Handles temporary capture files | Captures can contain sensitive data |

First say the radio scope in one sentence: *authorized SSID, channel, hardware, purpose, privacy rule, and cleanup.*

## Privacy and shared spectrum

| Situation | Correct response |
| --- | --- |
| Neighbor SSIDs appear in a scan | Ignore; do not record as targets |
| Client devices you do not own associate nearby | Do not target them |
| You only have a home guest SSID you administer | Document that SSID as authorized; keep purpose minimal |
| No authorized SSID available | Documentation-only practice; no capture |

Captures can include personal data. Prefer the minimum metadata needed for the lesson note. Delete temporary capture files after notes are saved unless you have a clear evidence retention reason in an authorized engagement.

## Tool mindset

Wireless tooling in Kali can list networks, set monitor mode, or capture handshakes in advanced labs. For this card:

1. Authorization text comes before adapter commands.
2. Purpose stays educational and minimal.
3. Privacy rule is written and followed.
4. Cleanup is mandatory.

If you are not sure the SSID is yours to test, you are done — stop.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Treating strong signal as permission
- Capturing “everything on the air” for practice
- Leaving capture files on shared disks
- Skipping hardware approval (broken or unauthorized adapters)
- Practicing on café / apartment / employer Wi‑Fi without written leave
- Expecting ASV Learn to provide a radio lab

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Authorization gate

Answer yes/no in `authorization_gate.txt`:

```text
i_own_or_have_written_permission_for_the_ssid=yes
ssid_label=ASV-LAB (replace with your authorized SSID or write NONE)
if_none=documentation_only_no_capture
```

If the answer is no / NONE, still complete Step 2 with the sample lab SSID as a **template only** and do not capture.

### Step 2 — Write the wireless test card

Create `wireless_test_card.txt`:

```text
authorized_ssid=ASV-LAB
channel=6
approved_hardware=lab wireless adapter
capture_purpose=document authorized lab handshake metadata only
privacy_rule=ignore non-lab networks and unrelated clients; do not store foreign SSIDs as targets
cleanup_note=delete temporary capture files after evidence notes are saved
out_of_scope=all SSIDs and clients not named ASV-LAB
```

Optional shell print:

```bash
authorized_ssid="ASV-LAB"
channel="6"
approved_hardware="lab wireless adapter"
capture_purpose="document authorized lab handshake metadata"
privacy_rule="ignore non-lab networks and unrelated clients"
cleanup_note="delete temporary capture files after evidence notes are saved"

printf '%s\n' \
  "ssid=$authorized_ssid" \
  "channel=$channel" \
  "hardware=$approved_hardware" \
  "purpose=$capture_purpose" \
  "privacy=$privacy_rule" \
  "cleanup=$cleanup_note"
```

### Step 3 — Self-review

- Is non-lab traffic explicitly excluded?
- Is cleanup concrete?
- If you lack authorization, did you stay documentation-only?

### Step 4 — One change you can explain

Tighten the privacy rule or capture purpose by one clause and say how that reduces risk to unrelated people.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| SSID | Network name broadcast by an access point |
| Channel | Radio channel used for the lab network |
| Capture | Recording wireless frames for analysis |
| Privacy rule | Written exclusion of unrelated networks/clients |
| Monitor mode | Adapter mode used in advanced wireless labs |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] Authorization gate answered honestly
- [ ] `wireless_test_card.txt` includes SSID, channel, hardware, purpose, privacy, cleanup
- [ ] Out-of-scope networks are excluded in writing
- [ ] No capture performed without authorization
- [ ] Temporary capture files (if any) deleted after notes

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Intercepting or attacking wireless networks without authorization can be illegal and invasive. Only practice on networks you own or have explicit written permission to test.

When those items are true, continue to **Forensics & Analysis**.

# Forensics & Analysis

## Why this lesson exists

Forensic work depends on **preservation** and careful language. Record what you observed, how you preserved the artifact, what you think it means, and what remains uncertain.

In this lesson you will write an evidence analysis card that separates observation from interpretation.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-08/{notes,evidence-copies}
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/stage-08
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-08\notes"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-08\evidence-copies"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\stage-08"
```

You will write `evidence_analysis_card.txt` under `notes/`. Work from **copies** in `evidence-copies/`, not from unique originals when originals must stay unchanged.

## Start here: preservation before interpretation

Do not explain evidence before protecting it. First name:

1. Evidence item / artifact identifier
2. Preservation step
3. Direct observation
4. Interpretation
5. Uncertainty
6. Next question

Forensic language should keep facts and conclusions separate so another reviewer can test your reasoning.

## Evidence discipline

| Field | Purpose | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Artifact identifier | Names the evidence item | Labels must be stable |
| Preservation step | Protects the original from accidental change | Working on the only copy is risky |
| Observation | What you can directly see | No hidden guesses |
| Interpretation | What the observation may mean | Marked as interpretation |
| Uncertainty | Assumptions kept visible | Required, not optional |
| Next question | Guides further analysis | Prevents false closure |

First say the evidence chain in one sentence: *artifact, preservation step, observation, interpretation, uncertainty, and next question.*

## Observation versus interpretation

| Type | Example | Where it goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observation | “Login failure events appear at 14:02–14:06 for user alex” | Observation |
| Interpretation | “Possible unauthorized access attempt in the training scenario” | Interpretation |
| Uncertainty | “Needs corroborating timestamps from another log source” | Uncertainty |
| Next question | “Which account and source generated the event?” | Next question |

If you cannot point to the bytes, line, or screenshot that supports a sentence, it is not yet an observation.

## Preservation habits for a small lab

| Habit | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Copy before analysis | Original stays unchanged |
| Note hash or size when practical | Detect accidental modification |
| Keep analysis notes separate from evidence copies | Avoid mixing commentary into artifacts |
| Record tool + version used for viewing | Reviewers can reproduce viewing conditions |
| Do not “clean up” the only copy | Cleanup belongs to scratch, not evidence |

Kali includes many analysis utilities. The tool name matters less than whether you can defend the chain: what you touched, what you saw, what you inferred.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Explaining before preserving
- Writing interpretation as fact
- Hiding uncertainty to sound confident
- Editing the only copy of a log or image
- Skipping the next question so analysis stops early
- Expecting ASV Learn to mount disk images for you in the lesson page

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Create a synthetic artifact

Write a tiny lab log copy (this is practice data, not a real incident):

`evidence-copies/lab-auth.log`

```text
2026-08-07T14:02:11Z FAIL user=alex src=10.0.3.44
2026-08-07T14:02:40Z FAIL user=alex src=10.0.3.44
2026-08-07T14:03:05Z FAIL user=alex src=10.0.3.44
2026-08-07T14:06:12Z SUCCESS user=alex src=10.0.3.44
```

Treat this file as the working copy. Imagine an original remains read-only elsewhere.

### Step 2 — Write the evidence analysis card

Create `notes/evidence_analysis_card.txt`:

```text
artifact_id=lab-image-001 / lab-auth.log working copy
preservation_step=work from evidence-copies/lab-auth.log; keep any original unchanged
observation=four auth events for user alex from 10.0.3.44 including three failures then one success
interpretation=possible unauthorized access attempt in the training scenario
uncertainty=needs corroborating timestamps from another log source; MFA status unknown
next_question=which account recovery or MFA signals exist around the same window
```

Optional shell print:

```bash
artifact_id="lab-image-001"
preservation_step="work from a copied artifact and keep the original unchanged"
observation="suspicious login event appears in the lab log"
interpretation="possible unauthorized access attempt in the training scenario"
uncertainty="needs corroborating timestamps from another log source"
next_question="which account and source generated the event"

printf '%s\n' \
  "artifact=$artifact_id" \
  "preservation=$preservation_step" \
  "observation=$observation" \
  "interpretation=$interpretation" \
  "uncertainty=$uncertainty" \
  "next_question=$next_question"
```

### Step 3 — Self-review

- Can a second analyst see what was directly observed?
- Is uncertainty visible?
- Did you avoid modifying the only imagined original?

### Step 4 — One change you can explain

Move one overconfident phrase from interpretation into uncertainty (or the reverse if you understated) and justify the edit.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Artifact | Evidence item under analysis |
| Preservation | Protecting originals from change |
| Observation | Directly seen fact |
| Interpretation | Possible meaning of the observation |
| Chain of custody | Record of who handled evidence and how |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] Working copy exists under `evidence-copies/`
- [ ] Analysis card separates observation and interpretation
- [ ] Uncertainty and next question are present
- [ ] Preservation step is written
- [ ] Only authorized / synthetic lab artifacts were used

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Analyze only artifacts you are authorized to handle. Do not acquire or inspect other people’s private data without legal authority and a clear case need.

When those items are true, continue to **Customizing Kali for Your Workflow**.

stages.title: Customizing Kali for Your Workflow

quiz.question: What should Kali customization improve?
options: Repeatability and evidence quality
Hidden shortcuts
Unreviewed tool use
Untracked files
quiz.explanation: Professional customization supports reproducible notes, evidence, and reporting.

quiz.question: What should exist before clever shell aliases?
options: A default that scans every discovered host

stages.content:
# Customizing Kali for Your Workflow

## Why this lesson exists

Customization should make lab work **repeatable**, easier to review, and easier to explain. A personal setup that hides evidence or depends on memory is not a professional workflow.

In this lesson you will write a workflow checklist: workspace layout, note template, tool profile, update habit, backup rule, and reviewer-ready summary.

A longer zero-to-job-ready Kali path exists outside this **20–25 hour** card; finish this checklist before expanding into that longer curriculum.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-kali-linux/{notes,evidence,reports,scratch}
cd ~/asv-learn-kali-linux
```

Windows (PowerShell on the host if notes live there):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\notes"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\evidence"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\reports"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux\scratch"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-kali-linux"
```

You will write `workflow_checklist.txt` in the course root folder.

## Start here: repeatability before shortcuts

Do not optimize for private shortcuts first. Name:

1. Workspace layout
2. Note template
3. Tool profile (defaults and boundaries)
4. Update habit
5. Backup rule
6. Reviewer-ready summary

Customization is useful when another reviewer can understand the setup. The goal is a repeatable lab workflow, not hidden convenience that only works from memory.

## Workflow checklist model

| Field | Professional reason | Failure mode if missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace layout | Separates notes, evidence, reports, scratch | Scratch mistaken for proof |
| Note template | Makes every run reproducible | Runs cannot be explained later |
| Tool profile | Documents defaults and scope boundaries | Accidental out-of-scope targets |
| Update habit | Keeps the lab snapshot current | Broken tools mid-engagement |
| Backup rule | Protects evidence and notes | Lost work after VM crash |
| Reviewer-ready summary | Turns practice into useful proof | Nobody can hand off findings |

First say the checklist in one sentence: *layout, note template, tool profile, update habit, backup rule, and reviewer summary.*

## Suggested layout

```text
~/asv-learn-kali-linux/
  notes/       # lab notes per stage
  evidence/    # saved tool output tied to notes
  reports/     # short findings for handoff
  scratch/     # disposable files; never the only copy of proof
```

Link each evidence file back to a note that states target, purpose, and time. A pile of screenshots without notes is not a workflow.

## Note template (minimum fields)

Use this for every future tool run:

```text
date=
authorized_target=
purpose=
command_or_action=
result_summary=
evidence_path=
next_action=
cleanup=
```

Aliases and shell functions are fine **after** this template exists. An alias that hides the target or skips the note is a downgrade.

## Tool profile boundaries

| Default | Boundary |
| --- | --- |
| Lab target variable | Always set to authorized label before scans |
| Output directory | Under `evidence/` with date prefix |
| Aggressive timing profiles | Off unless the note says why |
| Update commands | Run on a snapshot-friendly schedule |
| Wireless / exploit tools | Disabled or unused until their stage cards are complete |

Write the profile in plain language first. Implement aliases second.

## Update and backup

| Habit | Practical cadence for a learning lab |
| --- | --- |
| Snapshot before major package updates | Before `apt` big changes |
| Export notes/evidence after each practice block | End of session |
| Keep one offline or host-side backup of notes | Weekly or after each stage |
| Re-read scope note after restore | Snapshots can revive old assumptions |

## Common beginner mistakes

- Building clever aliases before a note template
- Saving everything in `/tmp` or Desktop clutter
- No backup until a VM disk fills
- Tool defaults that quietly expand scope
- Reviewer summary that lists tools instead of findings
- Treating this short card as the full multi-hundred-hour career path

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Create the folders

Ensure `notes`, `evidence`, `reports`, and `scratch` exist (commands above).

### Step 2 — Write the workflow checklist

Create `workflow_checklist.txt`:

```text
workspace_layout=~/asv-learn-kali-linux/{notes,evidence,reports,scratch}
note_template=date target purpose action result evidence_path next_action cleanup
tool_profile=safe defaults for authorized lab targets only; no aggressive profiles without a note
update_habit=snapshot then update lab packages before a new practice block
backup_rule=export notes and evidence to host storage after each lab session
reviewer_summary=finding summary with evidence path, impact, and remediation
longer_path_note=optional deeper curriculum exists beyond this 20-25h ASV Learn card; do not inflate this card hours
```

Optional shell setup print:

```bash
workspace_layout="$HOME/asv-learn-kali-linux/notes-evidence-reports-scratch"
note_template="target purpose output next-action"
tool_profile="safe aliases and defaults for authorized lab targets only"
update_habit="update the lab snapshot before a new practice block"
backup_rule="export notes and evidence after each lab"
reviewer_summary="finding summary with evidence, impact, and remediation"

mkdir -p "$HOME/asv-learn-kali-linux"/{notes,evidence,reports,scratch}
printf '%s\n' \
  "workspace_layout=$workspace_layout" \
  "note_template=$note_template" \
  "tool_profile=$tool_profile" \
  "update_habit=$update_habit" \
  "backup_rule=$backup_rule" \
  "reviewer_summary=$reviewer_summary"
```

### Step 3 — Self-review

- Could another person follow this without watching you type?
- Are scratch and evidence separated?
- Does the reviewer summary talk about findings, not ego?

### Step 4 — One change you can explain

Add one concrete alias or folder naming rule, then explain how it improves reviewability rather than speed alone.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Workspace layout | Where notes, evidence, reports, and scratch live |
| Note template | Required fields for every run |
| Tool profile | Intentional defaults and boundaries |
| Reviewer-ready summary | Handoff a second person can use |
| Repeatability | Same steps produce understandable results later |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] Folders for notes, evidence, reports, scratch exist
- [ ] `workflow_checklist.txt` covers all six fields
- [ ] Note template is copy-paste ready
- [ ] Backup rule is practical
- [ ] You can explain the setup in under two minutes
- [ ] You know this card is 20–25h, with a longer path available later

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

A customized Kali workflow does not grant permission. Keep every alias, script, and default pointed at authorized lab targets only.

When those items are true, you have finished this ASV Learn Kali card. Continue into deeper authorized labs or a longer curriculum when you are ready — without claiming those hours on this course card.

Use recon, scanning, and enumeration tools with scoped targets

Document tool output so another analyst can reproduce your steps
Keep lab practice separate from production systems and live targets
